evidence.quote: Lesions of the caudate nucleus rarely caused motor disorders but were more likely to cause behavioural problems. Chorea has been described in only 6% of those with caudate lesions, and dystonia in only 9%. The most significant behavioural disturbance described in 28% of those with caudate lesions was the syndrome of abulia, sometimes alternating with disinhibition (11%).
evidence.cite: Bhatia KP, Marsden CD. The behavioural and motor consequences of focal lesions of the basal ganglia in man. Brain. 1994;117(Pt 4):859-76.

data.title: Percent of caudate lesion cases with each problem

evidence.claim: Caudate neurons degenerate early in Huntington's disease
evidence.finding: In postmortem brains from 163 patients with Huntington's disease, the earliest changes were in the medial paraventricular caudate, the tail of the caudate and the dorsal putamen. Counts of caudate neurons showed 50% lost in grade 1 and 95% lost in grade 4. The grade correlated closely with clinical disability.
evidence.quote: The earliest changes were seen in the medial paraventricular portions of the caudate nucleus (CN), in the tail of the CN, and in the dorsal part of the putamen. Counts of neurons in the CN reveal that 50% are lost in grade 1 and that 95% are lost in grade 4
evidence.cite: Vonsattel JP, Myers RH, Stevens TJ, Ferrante RJ, Bird ED, Richardson EP Jr. Neuropathological classification of Huntington's disease. J Neuropathol Exp Neurol. 1985;44(6):559-77.

evidence.claim: The caudate and putamen support habit learning of associations
evidence.finding: Amnesic patients and non-demented Parkinson's disease patients did a probabilistic classification task. Amnesic patients learned the task normally, while Parkinson's patients failed to learn it despite intact memory for the training episode. The authors conclude the neostriatum, meaning the caudate and putamen, is essential for gradual habit learning.
evidence.quote: In contrast, patients with Parkinson's disease failed to learn the probabilistic classification task, despite having intact memory for the training episode. In humans, the neostriatum (caudate nucleus and putamen) is essential for the gradual, incremental learning of associations that is characteristic of habit learning.
evidence.cite: Knowlton BJ, Mangels JA, Squire LR. A neostriatal habit learning system in humans. Science. 1996;273(5280):1399-402.

evidence.claim: The caudate contributes to goal-directed learning and action selection
evidence.finding: Six epilepsy patients with depth electrodes learned associations between images and button presses, and three of them also received stimulation during feedback after correct responses. Caudate stimulation enhanced learning. The caudate and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex both showed more beta power after correct than incorrect trials.
evidence.quote: Three subjects participated in stimulation sessions during which caudate or putamen stimulation was delivered for some images during feedback after correct responses. Caudate stimulation enhanced learning.
evidence.cite: Bick SK, Patel SR, Katnani HA, et al. Caudate stimulation enhances learning. Brain. 2019;142(10):2930-2937.

stimulation.method: depth-electrode stimulation of the caudate during feedback (three of six patients)
stimulation.effect: Stimulating the caudate after correct responses improved how well patients learned image and button-press associations, and raised beta power in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex.
stimulation.quote: Caudate stimulation enhanced learning. Both caudate and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex demonstrated a beta power increase during the feedback period of the learning task that was greater following correct than incorrect trials.
stimulation.cite: Bick SK, Patel SR, Katnani HA, et al. Caudate stimulation enhances learning. Brain. 2019;142(10):2930-2937.

how_we_know: Autopsy measurements of dopamine in Parkinson's disease, lesion cases, and imaging during skill learning all point to a motor role for the putamen. Imaging is correlational, but the dopamine and lesion evidence is causal in direction. There is no good human stimulation study specific to the putamen.

evidence.claim: Loss of dopamine input to the putamen underlies the motor signs of Parkinson's disease
evidence.finding: The authors measured dopamine in striatum obtained at autopsy from eight patients with idiopathic Parkinson's disease. The putamen had nearly complete depletion in all subdivisions, with the caudal part lowest. They proposed that the motor deficits are mostly a consequence of dopamine loss in the putamen.
evidence.quote: we examined the pattern and degree of dopamine loss in striatum obtained at autopsy from eight patients with idiopathic Parkinson's disease. We found that in the putamen there was a nearly complete depletion of dopamine in all subdivisions, with the greatest reduction in the caudal portions (less than 1 percent of the dopamine remaining).
evidence.cite: Kish SJ, Shannak K, Hornykiewicz O. Uneven pattern of dopamine loss in the striatum of patients with idiopathic Parkinson's disease. Pathophysiologic and clinical implications. N Engl J Med. 1988;318(14):876-80.

evidence.claim: The putamen contributes to motor skill and sequence learning
evidence.finding: Fourteen healthy volunteers practiced a sequence of eight finger moves daily, and fMRI was done on days 1, 14 and 28. Activation in the rostrodorsal (associative) putamen decreased with practice, while activation in the caudoventral (sensorimotor) putamen increased. This suggests motor skills shift to the sensorimotor putamen as they become automatic.
evidence.quote: In both putamen, activation decreased with practice in rostrodorsal (associative) regions. In contrast, there was a significant signal increase in more caudoventral (sensorimotor) regions of the putamen.
evidence.cite: Lehéricy S, Benali H, Van de Moortele PF, et al. Distinct basal ganglia territories are engaged in early and advanced motor sequence learning. Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A. 2005;102(35):12566-71.

evidence.claim: Putaminal lesions commonly cause dystonia
evidence.finding: In the review of 240 reported cases, lesions of the lentiform nuclei commonly caused dystonia in 49% of cases, and in 63% when the putamen was involved. Abulia occurred in only 10% and disinhibition did not occur.
evidence.quote: Lesions of the lentiform nuclei rarely caused abulia (10%) and did not produce disinhibition, but they commonly caused dystonia (49%), particularly when the putamen was involved (63%).
evidence.cite: Bhatia KP, Marsden CD. The behavioural and motor consequences of focal lesions of the basal ganglia in man. Brain. 1994;117(Pt 4):859-76.

data.title: Percent of lentiform lesion cases with dystonia

how_we_know: Pallidal deep brain stimulation in randomized trials gives the strongest causal evidence for the motor role of the globus pallidus interna. Lesion reports and imaging during skill learning add support. These trials stimulate a diseased circuit, so they show what the structure can change, not what it does in a healthy brain.

evidence.claim: Bilateral pallidal damage causes parkinsonism and dystonia
evidence.finding: In the review of 240 reported cases with basal ganglia lesions, bilateral lentiform lesions, of either the globus pallidus or the putamen, infrequently caused parkinsonism in 19% and dystonia-parkinsonism in 6% of cases. The author concluded that these findings emphasize motor roles for putamen and globus pallidus.
evidence.quote: Bilateral lesions of the lentiform nuclei, either of the globus pallidus or of the putamen, caused parkinsonism (19%) or dystonia-parkinsonism (6%) infrequently. The frequent occurrence of dystonia and less commonly of parkinsonism with lentiform lesions emphasize the motor roles of putamen and globus pallidus.
evidence.cite: Bhatia KP, Marsden CD. The behavioural and motor consequences of focal lesions of the basal ganglia in man. Brain. 1994;117(Pt 4):859-76.

evidence.claim: The pallidum is engaged as motor skills become fast and automatic
evidence.finding: Fourteen healthy volunteers practiced a finger sequence over a month while fMRI was done. Faster reaction times were linked to signal changes in areas active at advanced learning stages, including the sensorimotor putamen and globus pallidus. This is correlational.
evidence.quote: reaction time (movement speed) was negatively correlated with signal changes in areas activated during advanced learning stages, including the sensorimotor putamen and globus pallidus.
evidence.cite: Lehéricy S, Benali H, Van de Moortele PF, et al. Distinct basal ganglia territories are engaged in early and advanced motor sequence learning. Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A. 2005;102(35):12566-71.

evidence.claim: Pallidal deep brain stimulation reduces dystonia
evidence.finding: In a controlled multicenter study, 22 patients with primary generalized dystonia received bilateral stimulation of the internal globus pallidus. The mean dystonia movement score improved from 46.3 before surgery to 21.0 at 12 months. A blinded video review and a double-blind on-off test at three months supported the benefit.
evidence.quote: The dystonia movement score improved from a mean (+/-SD) of 46.3+/-21.3 before surgery to 21.0+/-14.1 at 12 months (P<0.001).
evidence.cite: Vidailhet M, Vercueil L, Houeto JL, et al. Bilateral deep-brain stimulation of the globus pallidus in primary generalized dystonia. N Engl J Med. 2005;352(5):459-67.

evidence.claim: Pallidal stimulation improves motor function in Parkinson's disease, similar to subthalamic stimulation
evidence.finding: In 13 hospitals, 299 patients with Parkinson's disease were randomly assigned to pallidal or subthalamic stimulation. Motor improvement was similar with either target at 24 months. Serious adverse events occurred in 51% of pallidal and 56% of subthalamic patients.
evidence.quote: Serious adverse events occurred in 51% of patients undergoing pallidal stimulation and in 56% of those undergoing subthalamic stimulation, with no significant between-group differences at 24 months. Patients with Parkinson's disease had similar improvement in motor function after either pallidal or subthalamic stimulation.
evidence.cite: Follett KA, Weaver FM, Stern M, et al. Pallidal versus subthalamic deep-brain stimulation for Parkinson's disease. N Engl J Med. 2010;362(22):2077-91.

stimulation.method: bilateral deep brain stimulation of the internal globus pallidus (22 patients)
stimulation.effect: In patients with generalized dystonia, stimulation reduced involuntary movements, and scores were better with the stimulator on than off.
stimulation.quote: At three months, patients underwent a double-blind evaluation in the presence and absence of neurostimulation. At the three-month evaluation, dystonia movement scores were significantly better with neurostimulation than without neurostimulation (24.6+/-17.7 vs. 34.6+/-12.3, P<0.001).
stimulation.cite: Vidailhet M, Vercueil L, Houeto JL, et al. Bilateral deep-brain stimulation of the globus pallidus in primary generalized dystonia. N Engl J Med. 2005;352(5):459-67.

how_we_know: Imaging shows accumbens activation when people anticipate rewards, and recordings in monkeys show dopamine neurons coding prediction errors. Deep brain stimulation of the accumbens in small trials shows that changing its activity can relieve anhedonia and obsessive-compulsive symptoms. The dopamine recordings are from monkeys and the stimulation trials are small and in patients.

evidence.claim: The accumbens responds to anticipated rewards, not to anticipated punishments
evidence.finding: In eight healthy volunteers, event-related fMRI was recorded during anticipation of increasing monetary rewards and punishments. Anticipating larger rewards raised both self-reported happiness and accumbens activation, while anticipating larger punishments did neither. A different striatal region, the medial caudate, responded to both.
evidence.quote: Whereas anticipation of increasing rewards elicited both increasing self-reported happiness and NAcc activation, anticipation of increasing punishment elicited neither. However, anticipation of both rewards and punishments activated a different striatal region (the medial caudate).
evidence.cite: Knutson B, Adams CM, Fong GW, Hommer D. Anticipation of increasing monetary reward selectively recruits nucleus accumbens. J Neurosci. 2001;21(16):RC159.

evidence.claim: Dopamine signals reward prediction and prediction errors
evidence.finding: This review combines recordings from dopamine neurons in the primate with computational theory. The neurons' changing output appears to signal errors in the prediction of future rewards. It is recorded in monkeys and reviewed alongside learning theory, not measured in the accumbens itself.
evidence.quote: Physiological work has recently complemented these studies by identifying dopaminergic neurons in the primate whose fluctuating output apparently signals changes or errors in the predictions of future salient and rewarding events.
evidence.cite: Schultz W, Dayan P, Montague PR. A neural substrate of prediction and reward. Science. 1997;275(5306):1593-9.

evidence.claim: The accumbens is a deep brain stimulation target in obsessive-compulsive disorder
evidence.finding: Sixteen patients with treatment-refractory OCD received bilateral accumbens stimulation. In the open phase the mean Y-BOCS score fell by 46%, from 33.7 to 18.0 after 8 months, and nine of 16 patients were responders. A double-blind sham-controlled phase in 14 patients confirmed a difference between active and sham stimulation.
evidence.quote: In the open phase, the mean (SD) Y-BOCS score decreased by 46%, from 33.7 (3.6) at baseline to 18.0 (11.4) after 8 months (P < .001). Nine of 16 patients were responders, with a mean (SD) Y-BOCS score decrease of 23.7 (7.0), or 72%.
evidence.cite: Denys D, Mantione M, Figee M, et al. Deep brain stimulation of the nucleus accumbens for treatment-refractory obsessive-compulsive disorder. Arch Gen Psychiatry. 2010;67(10):1061-8.

evidence.claim: Blunted accumbens activity accompanies anhedonia, and stimulation relieves it
evidence.finding: Three patients with extremely resistant depression received bilateral accumbens stimulation, with settings changed in a double-blind way. Ratings improved in all three with the stimulator on and worsened in all three when it was turned off. FDG-PET showed metabolic changes in frontostriatal networks.
evidence.quote: Clinical ratings improved in all three patients when the stimulator was on, and worsened in all three patients when the stimulator was turned off.
evidence.cite: Schlaepfer TE, Cohen MX, Frick C, et al. Deep brain stimulation to reward circuitry alleviates anhedonia in refractory major depression. Neuropsychopharmacology. 2008;33(2):368-77.

stimulation.method: bilateral deep brain stimulation of the nucleus accumbens (three patients with depression)
stimulation.effect: Clinical ratings of depression improved when the stimulator was on and worsened when it was off, with no side effects beyond the surgery.
stimulation.quote: Clinical ratings improved in all three patients when the stimulator was on, and worsened in all three patients when the stimulator was turned off. Effects were observable immediately, and no side effects occurred in any of the patients.
stimulation.cite: Schlaepfer TE, Cohen MX, Frick C, et al. Deep brain stimulation to reward circuitry alleviates anhedonia in refractory major depression. Neuropsychopharmacology. 2008;33(2):368-77.

how_we_know: The core evidence is lesion work: the surgical case of H.M. and later patients with damage confined to the hippocampus. Imaging of London taxi drivers shows the hippocampus can change with experience, and recordings in epilepsy patients find cells tied to place. Stimulation of the medial temporal lobe has produced mixed results, with impairment in a larger study and improvement in a smaller one.

evidence.claim: Bilateral hippocampal removal in H.M. caused profound anterograde amnesia
evidence.finding: Scoville and Milner tested nine patients, eight psychotic and one epileptic, after bilateral medial temporal resection. Memory impairment was persistent when the removal reached the anterior hippocampus and hippocampal gyrus, and its severity depended on how much hippocampus was removed. Early memories and technical skills were intact.
evidence.quote: Bilateral medial temporal lobe resection in man results in a persistent impairment of recent memory whenever the removal is carried far enough posteriorly to damage portions of the anterior hippocampus and hippocampal gyrus.
evidence.cite: Scoville WB, Milner B. Loss of recent memory after bilateral hippocampal lesions. 1957. J Neuropsychiatry Clin Neurosci. 2000;12(1):103-13 (reprint of the 1957 paper).

evidence.claim: A lesion limited to the hippocampus is enough to cause amnesia
evidence.finding: Patient R.B. developed memory impairment after an ischemic episode and was followed for five years until his death. He had marked anterograde amnesia and little retrograde amnesia without other cognitive impairment. His brain showed a circumscribed bilateral lesion of the entire CA1 field of the hippocampus.
evidence.quote: During the 5 years until his death, R.B. exhibited marked anterograde amnesia, little if any retrograde amnesia, and showed no signs of cognitive impairment other than memory. Thorough histological examination revealed a circumscribed bilateral lesion involving the entire CA1 field of the hippocampus.
evidence.cite: Zola-Morgan S, Squire LR, Amaral DG. Human amnesia and the medial temporal region: enduring memory impairment following a bilateral lesion limited to field CA1 of the hippocampus. J Neurosci. 1986;6(10):2950-67.

evidence.claim: The posterior hippocampus supports spatial memory and can change with experience
evidence.finding: Structural MRI of licensed London taxi drivers was compared with that of control subjects who did not drive taxis. The posterior hippocampi of taxi drivers were significantly larger, and a more anterior region was larger in controls. Volume correlated with time spent as a taxi driver, positively in the posterior and negatively in the anterior hippocampus.
evidence.quote: The posterior hippocampi of taxi drivers were significantly larger relative to those of control subjects. A more anterior hippocampal region was larger in control subjects than in taxi drivers. Hippocampal volume correlated with the amount of time spent as a taxi driver (positively in the posterior and negatively in the anterior hippocampus).
evidence.cite: Maguire EA, Gadian DG, Johnsrude IS, et al. Navigation-related structural change in the hippocampi of taxi drivers. Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A. 2000;97(8):4398-403.

evidence.claim: Place-responsive cells in the human hippocampus support navigation
evidence.finding: The authors recorded from 317 neurons in the human medial temporal and frontal lobes while patients navigated a virtual town. Some cells responded at specific spatial locations, mainly in the hippocampus, and others responded to views of landmarks, mainly in the parahippocampal region.
evidence.quote: We directly recorded from 317 neurons in the human medial temporal and frontal lobes while subjects explored and navigated a virtual town. Here we present evidence for a neural code of human spatial navigation based on cells that respond at specific spatial locations and cells that respond to views of landmarks. The former are present primarily in the hippocampus, and the latter in the parahippocampal region.
evidence.cite: Ekstrom AD, Kahana MJ, Caplan JB, et al. Cellular networks underlying human spatial navigation. Nature. 2003;425(6954):184-8.

stimulation.method: 50 Hz electrical stimulation of the entorhinal region and hippocampus during encoding
stimulation.effect: In neurosurgical patients, stimulation during encoding made memory worse on both spatial and verbal tasks.
stimulation.quote: In contrast to earlier work, electrical stimulation impaired memory performance significantly in both spatial and verbal tasks. Stimulation in both the entorhinal region and hippocampus caused decreased memory performance.
stimulation.cite: Jacobs J, Miller J, Lee SA, et al. Direct electrical stimulation of the human entorhinal region and hippocampus impairs memory. Neuron. 2016;92(5):983-990.

how_we_know: Rare patients with selective bilateral amygdala damage, such as S.M., give the causal evidence, together with stimulation in epilepsy patients and fMRI and PET studies of fear. Kluver and Bucy's 1939 monkey lesions, which first showed placidity and hyperorality, predate the PubMed abstracts used here. Imaging cannot say whether the amygdala is required, and lesion patients are very few.

evidence.claim: Bilateral amygdala damage impairs the induction and experience of fear
evidence.finding: Patient S.M., with focal bilateral amygdala lesions, was exposed to live snakes and spiders, a haunted house and emotionally evocative films. She never showed fear and never reported more than minimal fear, across questionnaires and three months of experience sampling. She could show and feel other basic emotions.
evidence.quote: we conducted a new study in a rare human patient, SM, who has focal bilateral amygdala lesions. To provoke fear in SM, we exposed her to live snakes and spiders, took her on a tour of a haunted house, and showed her emotionally evocative films. On no occasion did SM exhibit fear, and she never endorsed feeling more than minimal levels of fear.
evidence.cite: Feinstein JS, Adolphs R, Damasio A, Tranel D. The human amygdala and the induction and experience of fear. Curr Biol. 2011;21(1):34-8.

evidence.claim: Bilateral amygdala damage impairs recognition of fearful faces
evidence.finding: Working with one rare patient with selective bilateral amygdala damage, the authors found the amygdala may be indispensable for recognizing fear in facial expressions and for recognizing multiple emotions in one expression. It is not needed to recognize who a person is from a face.
evidence.quote: Here, with the help of one such rare patient, we report findings that suggest the human amygdala may be indispensable to: (1) recognize fear in facial expressions; (2) recognize multiple emotions in a single facial expression; but (3) is not required to recognize personal identity from faces.
evidence.cite: Adolphs R, Tranel D, Damasio H, Damasio A. Impaired recognition of emotion in facial expressions following bilateral damage to the human amygdala. Nature. 1994;372(6507):669-72.

evidence.claim: The amygdala is needed for fear conditioning, the hippocampus for the declarative facts
evidence.finding: A patient with selective bilateral amygdala damage did not acquire conditioned autonomic responses but did learn the facts about which sounds or images were paired with the shock. A patient with selective hippocampal damage showed the opposite pattern, and a patient with damage to both acquired neither.
evidence.quote: A patient with selective bilateral damage to the amygdala did not acquire conditioned autonomic responses to visual or auditory stimuli but did acquire the declarative facts about which visual or auditory stimuli were paired with the unconditioned stimulus. By contrast, a patient with selective bilateral damage to the hippocampus failed to acquire the facts but did acquire the conditioning.
evidence.cite: Bechara A, Tranel D, Damasio H, Adolphs R, Rockland C, Damasio AR. Double dissociation of conditioning and declarative knowledge relative to the amygdala and hippocampus in humans. Science. 1995;269(5227):1115-8.

evidence.claim: The amygdala reads the emotional significance of faces
evidence.finding: Positron emission tomography was recorded while subjects viewed fearful or happy faces of varying intensity. The response in the left amygdala was significantly greater to fearful than to happy expressions, and it grew as fear increased. This is correlational evidence.
evidence.quote: Positron-emission tomography (PET) measures of neural activity were acquired while subjects viewed photographs of fearful or happy faces, varying systematically in emotional intensity. The neuronal response in the left amygdala was significantly greater to fearful as opposed to happy expressions.
evidence.cite: Morris JS, Frith CD, Perrett DI, et al. A differential neural response in the human amygdala to fearful and happy facial expressions. Nature. 1996;383(6603):812-5.

stimulation.method: direct electrical stimulation through intracerebral electrodes in epilepsy patients
stimulation.effect: Stimulating the right amygdala induced negative emotions, mainly fear and sadness, while stimulating the left could produce either pleasant or unpleasant emotions.
stimulation.quote: According to responses on Izard scales, electrical stimulations of the right amygdala induced negative emotions, especially fear and sadness. In contrast, stimulations of the left amygdala were able to induce either pleasant (happiness) or unpleasant (fear, anxiety, sadness) emotions.
stimulation.cite: Lanteaume L, Khalfa S, Régis J, Marquis P, Chauvel P, Bartolomei F. Emotion induction after direct intracerebral stimulations of human amygdala. Cereb Cortex. 2007;17(6):1307-13.

how_we_know: The ventricles are known from anatomy and physiology, and the best abstract-level evidence concerns what happens when they enlarge or when fluid flow fails. Meta-analyses of MRI show ventricular enlargement in disease, and surgical series show that draining excess fluid helps hydrocephalus. The classic measurements of CSF production by the choroid plexus predate abstracts on PubMed and are not quoted here.

evidence.claim: Lateral ventricles enlarge when surrounding brain tissue is lost, as in schizophrenia
evidence.finding: A meta-analysis of 58 MRI studies included 1,588 patients with schizophrenia. Taking controls as 100%, total ventricular volume was 126% and the bodies of the lateral ventricles were 116%, while cerebral volume was 98%. The ventricles therefore differed more than the brain did.
evidence.quote: Assuming a volume of 100% in the comparison group, they found that the mean cerebral volume of the subjects with schizophrenia was smaller (98%), but the mean total ventricular volume of the subjects with schizophrenia was greater (126%). Relative to the global ventricular system differences, the largest differences in ventricular subdivisions were in the right and left body of the lateral ventricle, where the volumes of schizophrenic subjects were 116% and 116%, respectively.
evidence.cite: Wright IC, Rabe-Hesketh S, Woodruff PW, David AS, Murray RM, Bullmore ET. Meta-analysis of regional brain volumes in schizophrenia. Am J Psychiatry. 2000;157(1):16-25.

evidence.claim: Normal pressure hydrocephalus is treatable by draining excess cerebrospinal fluid
evidence.finding: A systematic review covered 64 studies of 3,063 patients with idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus who had shunt surgery. On average 71% improved with 1% mortality, and in the last five years of studies 82% improved with 0.2% mortality. This shows that the symptoms depend on fluid dynamics, although patients must be selected carefully.
evidence.quote: Positive improvement following shunt insertion was reported in an average of 71 % of patients with an average 1 % mortality. Results from studies published in the last 5 years showed 82 % improvement following shunt insertion, mortality of 0.2 %, and combined common complications rate of 8.2 %.
evidence.cite: Toma AK, Papadopoulos MC, Stapleton S, Kitchen ND, Watkins LD. Systematic review of the outcome of shunt surgery in idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus. Acta Neurochir (Wien). 2013;155(10):1977-80.

data.title: Percent of shunted patients who improved

evidence.claim: Cerebrospinal fluid clears waste from the brain
evidence.finding: In mice, in vivo two-photon imaging of fluorescent tracers showed that CSF enters the brain along spaces around penetrating arteries. Interstitial fluid was cleared along paravenous pathways. Mice lacking the aquaporin-4 water channel had about 70% less interstitial solute clearance, and clearance of amyloid beta was reduced. These are animal data.
evidence.quote: On the basis of in vivo two-photon imaging of small fluorescent tracers, we showed that CSF enters the parenchyma along paravascular spaces that surround penetrating arteries and that brain interstitial fluid is cleared along paravenous drainage pathways.
evidence.cite: Iliff JJ, Wang M, Liao Y, et al. A paravascular pathway facilitates CSF flow through the brain parenchyma and the clearance of interstitial solutes, including amyloid β. Sci Transl Med. 2012;4(147):147ra111.

how_we_know: Autopsy studies of Parkinson's and Huntington's disease show which parts of the striatum fail in each, and resting-state fMRI in 1,000 people maps how the cortex connects to it. Deep brain stimulation near the ventral striatum shows it can be modulated in patients with obsessive-compulsive disorder. The direct and indirect pathway model comes mainly from animal work and is not tested in these studies.

evidence.claim: Cortex and thalamus project to the striatum in topographic loops
evidence.finding: Resting-state fMRI data from 1,000 subjects were used to map each striatal voxel to its most strongly correlated cortical network. At least five cortical zones in the striatum were linked to sensorimotor, premotor, limbic and two association networks, with a topography consistent with monkey anatomy. Most of the human striatum was coupled to association networks.
evidence.quote: Data from 1,000 subjects were registered with nonlinear deformation of the striatum in combination with surface-based alignment of the cerebral cortex. The results revealed at least five cortical zones in the striatum linked to sensorimotor, premotor, limbic, and two association networks with a topography globally consistent with monkey anatomical studies.
evidence.cite: Choi EY, Yeo BT, Buckner RL. The organization of the human striatum estimated by intrinsic functional connectivity. J Neurophysiol. 2012;108(8):2242-63.

evidence.claim: Loss of dopamine from the dorsal striatum causes Parkinson's disease
evidence.finding: Dopamine was measured in striatum from eight patients with Parkinson's disease at autopsy. The putamen had nearly complete depletion in all subdivisions, with less than 1 percent remaining in the caudal part. In the caudate only the most dorsal rostral part was severely depleted, with 4 percent remaining.
evidence.quote: We found that in the putamen there was a nearly complete depletion of dopamine in all subdivisions, with the greatest reduction in the caudal portions (less than 1 percent of the dopamine remaining). In the caudate nucleus, the only subdivision with severe dopamine reduction was the most dorsal rostral part (4 percent of the dopamine remaining); the other subdivisions still had substantial levels of dopamine (up to approximately 40 percent of control levels).
evidence.cite: Kish SJ, Shannak K, Hornykiewicz O. Uneven pattern of dopamine loss in the striatum of patients with idiopathic Parkinson's disease. Pathophysiologic and clinical implications. N Engl J Med. 1988;318(14):876-80.

evidence.claim: Loss of medium spiny neurons causes Huntington's disease with chorea
evidence.finding: Postmortem brains from 163 patients with Huntington's disease showed marked variation in how severely the striatum was affected. The authors set up a five-grade scale (0 to 4) that correlated closely with clinical disability. Neuron counts in the caudate showed 50% lost at grade 1 and 95% at grade 4.
evidence.quote: In postmortem brain specimens from 163 clinically diagnosed cases of Huntington's disease (HD) the striatum exhibited marked variation in the severity of neuropathological involvement. The grade correlates closely with the extent of clinical disability as assessed by a rating scale.
evidence.cite: Vonsattel JP, Myers RH, Stevens TJ, Ferrante RJ, Bird ED, Richardson EP Jr. Neuropathological classification of Huntington's disease. J Neuropathol Exp Neurol. 1985;44(6):559-77.

evidence.claim: Striatal dysfunction is associated with obsessive-compulsive disorder
evidence.finding: Four teams combined their long-term results of deep brain stimulation at the ventral internal capsule and adjacent ventral striatum for severe, treatment-resistant OCD. About two-thirds of patients had clinically significant symptom reductions and functional improvement. Results improved as the target moved to a more posterior site near the ventral striatum.
evidence.quote: Here, we present combined long-term results of those studies, which reveal clinically significant symptom reductions and functional improvement in about two-thirds of patients.
evidence.cite: Greenberg BD, Gabriels LA, Malone DA Jr, et al. Deep brain stimulation of the ventral internal capsule/ventral striatum for obsessive-compulsive disorder: worldwide experience. Mol Psychiatry. 2010;15(1):64-79.

stimulation.method: deep brain stimulation of the ventral internal capsule and ventral striatum (combined series)
stimulation.effect: In patients with severe obsessive-compulsive disorder, stimulation reduced symptoms and improved function in about two-thirds.
stimulation.quote: Psychiatric neurosurgery teams in the United States and Europe have studied deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the ventral anterior limb of the internal capsule and adjacent ventral striatum (VC/VS) for severe and highly treatment-resistant obsessive-compulsive disorder. Here, we present combined long-term results of those studies, which reveal clinically significant symptom reductions and functional improvement in about two-thirds of patients.
stimulation.cite: Greenberg BD, Gabriels LA, Malone DA Jr, et al. Deep brain stimulation of the ventral internal capsule/ventral striatum for obsessive-compulsive disorder: worldwide experience. Mol Psychiatry. 2010;15(1):64-79.

how_we_know: Lesions and stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus first tested the circuit model in monkeys and then in people, and randomized trials of stimulation in Parkinson's disease now give strong evidence. Studies of Parkinson's patients show that the striatum supports habit learning. The pathway model itself is mostly built from animal work, so human studies test its predictions rather than the wiring.

evidence.claim: A lesion of the subthalamic nucleus reduces parkinsonian signs in monkeys
evidence.finding: Monkeys were made parkinsonian with MPTP, and the subthalamic nucleus was then lesioned. The lesions reduced all of the major motor disturbances in the opposite limbs, including akinesia, rigidity and tremor. This supported the idea that excess subthalamic activity drives parkinsonism.
evidence.quote: To test this hypothesis, the effects of lesions of the subthalamic nucleus were evaluated in monkeys rendered parkinsonian by treatment with 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP). The lesions reduced all of the major motor disturbances in the contralateral limbs, including akinesia, rigidity, and tremor.
evidence.cite: Bergman H, Wichmann T, DeLong MR. Reversal of experimental parkinsonism by lesions of the subthalamic nucleus. Science. 1990;249(4975):1436-8.

evidence.claim: The basal ganglia contribute to habit learning and procedural memory
evidence.finding: Amnesic patients and non-demented Parkinson's disease patients did a probabilistic classification task. Amnesic patients learned the task normally but remembered the training episode poorly. Parkinson's patients failed to learn despite intact memory of the episode, a double dissociation.
evidence.quote: Amnesic patients exhibited normal learning of the task but had severely impaired declarative memory for the training episode. In contrast, patients with Parkinson's disease failed to learn the probabilistic classification task, despite having intact memory for the training episode.
evidence.cite: Knowlton BJ, Mangels JA, Squire LR. A neostriatal habit learning system in humans. Science. 1996;273(5280):1399-402.

evidence.claim: Subthalamic stimulation improves Parkinson's disease beyond medication alone
evidence.finding: In a randomized-pairs trial, 156 patients with advanced Parkinson's disease received subthalamic stimulation plus medication or medical management alone. After six months, stimulation improved quality of life by 9.5 points and motor severity by 19.6 points more than medication alone. Serious adverse events were more common with stimulation, 13% versus 4%.
evidence.quote: Pairwise comparisons showed that neurostimulation, as compared with medication alone, caused greater improvements from baseline to six months in the PDQ-39 (50 of 78 pairs, P=0.02) and the UPDRS-III (55 of 78, P<0.001), with mean improvements of 9.5 and 19.6 points, respectively.
evidence.cite: Deuschl G, Schade-Brittinger C, Krack P, et al. A randomized trial of deep-brain stimulation for Parkinson's disease. N Engl J Med. 2006;355(9):896-908.

data.title: Extra improvement with stimulation over medication

evidence.claim: A lesion or stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus affects tremor, rigidity and ballism
evidence.finding: Bilateral subthalamic stimulation was tested in three patients with disabling akinetic-rigid Parkinson's disease. Three months after surgery activities-of-daily-living scores improved by 58 to 88% and motor scores by 42 to 84%. In one patient, stimulation could induce ballism, which stopped when stimulation was reduced.
evidence.quote: 3 months after surgery, activities of daily living scores had improved by 58-88% and motor scores by 42-84%. In one patient, stimulation could induce ballism that was stopped by reduction of stimulation.
evidence.cite: Limousin P, Pollak P, Benazzouz A, et al. Effect of parkinsonian signs and symptoms of bilateral subthalamic nucleus stimulation. Lancet. 1995;345(8942):91-5.

stimulation.method: bilateral deep brain stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus (three patients)
stimulation.effect: Stimulation improved motor scores in Parkinson's disease and, in one patient, could induce ballism that stopped when the stimulation was reduced.
stimulation.quote: 3 months after surgery, activities of daily living scores had improved by 58-88% and motor scores by 42-84%. In one patient, stimulation could induce ballism that was stopped by reduction of stimulation.
stimulation.cite: Limousin P, Pollak P, Benazzouz A, et al. Effect of parkinsonian signs and symptoms of bilateral subthalamic nucleus stimulation. Lancet. 1995;345(8942):91-5.
